newsitem.title: GERMANY: INTERVIEW-Welteke says no move yet on revaluing fx.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Welteke says no move yet on revaluing fx.

text.p: Three weeks after firmly rejecting Bonn's plans to revalue its gold assets, the Bundesbank said it would consider revaluing currency reserves but stressed on Tuesday that no firm decisions had been reached.
"No final decisions have been taken," Ernst Welteke told Reuters in an interview, answering questions about possible Bundesbank plans to revalue its currency reserves.

Earlier on Tuesday, Bonn government sources said the Bundesbank would be willing to revalue its dollar reserves at 1.50 marks or higher after having valued these at 1.3620 marks in last year's balance sheet.
The Bundesbank, following general German business practices, values its currency reserves at historic foreign exchange rate lows.

Welteke, underscoring relations between Bonn and the Frankfurt-based Bundesbank had normalised as the recent weeks' unusually public gold row had been settled, also stressed the Bundesbank would make the decision on currencies alone.

"After the issue of revaluing gold reserves had been removed from the agenda, there was the question of what we would do with the currency reserves and whether we might be able to revalue currency reserves," Welteke said. "This issue falls within our jursidiction."

Welteke, also president of the state central bank in Hesse, minced no words in explaining the Bundesbank would not abandon the caution that prevades all policy decisions or allow others to meddle in its activities.

"The central bank council has signalled its willingness to revalue the dollar differently in the 1997 balance sheet, but the council reserves the right to decide how it might use profits that could result from this," Welteke said.
To revalue currency assets, most of which are in dollars, Welteke said the Bundesbank would carefully monitor developments and then, make an appropriate decision.
Usually, the central bank transfers a portion of its profits from the previous year in April of the following year to the Bonn government, which uses the funds to help pare back debt.

But next year, Welteke suggested the Bundesbank might consider releasing its balance a little later to avoid any conflict with the decision on which nations will be able to enter currency union in 1999.

Since part of the Bundesbank's reason for rejecting Bonn's gold plan was to keep Germany from indulging in the creative accounting practices it had chastised others for, the central bank will likely make sure no extra money flows to Bonn before the final decision on currency union membership is taken.

"The timing might be a bit difficult (next year) as the decision on EMU (economic and monetary union) membership is expected to be taken in May. We could consider possibly delaying the release of the balance sheet," Welteke said. "The world is not going to come to an end if the Bundesbank, in light of the issue, decides to release its balance sheet one month later."

The assets could be revalued in one of two ways, Welteke said, explaining the Bundesbank could either value currencies at their purchase price, or if that price exceeds current values, at actual levels.
"Of course, we will continue to excercise the principle of caution," he added.

Possible profits resulting from such a revaluation would differ from non-realised profits achieved through any revaluation of gold reserves, Welteke said. "Profits that could occur through this would not be comparable to anything from a gold revaluation," Welteke said.

"These profits could be used to alter the format of the balance sheet, to create risk provisions that one would be able to assess after the members of Europe's monetary union have been decided, or to payout to the Finance Ministry as part of the traditional transfer," Welteke said.

While technical aspects of a currency revaluation appear clear, and Bonn has said it would hold further talks with the Bundesbank on the issue, Welteke indicated the Bundesbank was not under any pressure to decide the issue soon or make a formal announcement about it.
